title: A2LA SOC 2 Accreditation: What It Means for Audits
metaDescription: BARR Advisory earns A2LA accreditation for SOC 2 audits. Discover what rising auditor standards mean for your evidence collection and compliance.
excerpt: As audit firms gain formal A2LA accreditation for SOC 2 examinations, compliance teams must prepare for deeper scrutiny across Trust Services Criteria.
content:
When enterprise procurement teams ask for a SOC 2 Type II report, they expect an airtight, defensible assurance that your security controls actually function in practice. Yet compliance officers know that audit rigor can vary drastically depending on an assessor’s internal methodologies. That baseline is beginning to tighten across the industry. In a notable development reported by 01net, BARR Advisory achieved formal accreditation from the American Association for Laboratory Accreditation (A2LA) specifically for conducting SOC 2 examinations.

While CPA firms have traditionally operated under AICPA guidelines, external accreditation under international quality benchmarks—specifically ISO/IEC 17020 for inspection bodies—brings a structured layer of oversight to how audits are scoped, executed, and documented. For security and compliance teams preparing for upcoming audit cycles, this shift highlights a critical operational reality: as the auditors themselves face higher scrutiny, your internal control evidence must be cleaner, faster, and more verifiable than ever.

Why Auditor Accreditation Raises the Scrutiny Bar

Under traditional AICPA attestation standards (specifically AT-C 205), CPA firms maintain professional responsibility for their assertions. However, third-party accreditation introduces standardized peer and technical reviews of the auditing organization itself. For compliance officers, this dynamic transforms what happens during fieldwork in several tangible ways:

  • Exhaustive Population Sampling: Accredited inspection bodies must demonstrate rigorous sampling methodologies. Auditors will demand complete population files—such as complete lists of production code commits or offboarded personnel—rather than accepting pre-filtered samples from management.
  • Uncompromising Observation Windows: For a SOC 2 Type II report, maintaining control consistency across a 3-, 6-, or 12-month period is vital. Greater auditor oversight means smaller tolerances for control gaps, delayed reviews, or missing tickets.
  • Objective Technical Validation: Assessments of technical safeguards, such as role-based access control (RBAC) configurations and encryption baselines, will adhere more strictly to empirical verification over subjective policy reviews.

Control Areas Demanding Tighter Evidence Preparation

As audit firms adjust their internal quality management systems to meet accreditation mandates, compliance teams should proactively audit-proof their controls before fieldwork begins. Priority should be given to the Common Criteria (Security), along with any additional scoped Trust Services Criteria:

  • Change Management (CC8.1): Move away from static screenshots of tickets. Auditors will verify traceability from initial Jira/ticket requests to pull request approvals, automated CI/CD pipeline tests, and production deployment logs.
  • Access Governance (CC6.1 - CC6.3): User access reviews must show definitive evidence of quarterly reviews, immediate offboarding (typically within 24-48 hours), and multi-factor authentication (MFA) enforcement across all production and corporate infrastructure.
  • Incident Response & Monitoring (CC7.2 - CC7.4): Ensure audit trails document not just that alerts fired, but that alerts were investigated, triaged, and closed according to your stated SLAs.

Harmonizing SOC 2 with ISO 27001, HIPAA, and CMMC

An increasingly rigorous SOC 2 examination does not require reinventing your internal compliance wheel. Much of the evidence collected for an accredited SOC 2 assessor directly maps to other critical frameworks:

  • ISO/IEC 27001:2022: Controls within Annex A—such as A.5.15 (Access Control), A.8.8 (Management of Technical Vulnerabilities), and A.8.9 (Configuration Management)—directly correspond to SOC 2 CC6, CC7, and CC8 controls.
  • HIPAA Security Rule: Administrative and technical safeguards defined in 45 CFR § 164.308 and § 164.312 closely track the Common Criteria and Confidentiality trust services criteria.
  • CMMC Level 2: NIST SP 800-171 practices surrounding Access Control (AC) and System and Information Integrity (SI) rely on the same continuous monitoring logs required during a Type II observation period.

Actionable Next Steps for Compliance Leaders

The rise of formal auditor accreditation signals a healthier compliance ecosystem. It reduces the prevalence of superficial audits and restores enterprise trust in assurance reports. However, it also eliminates the margin for error during evidence gathering.

To prepare your organization for higher audit rigor, transition your processes away from manual point-in-time evidence collection toward automated, continuous monitoring.
